title: Is computer addiction a thing?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether computer addiction is a real condition, covering online porn, gaming, social media, and Internet Addiction Disorder (not officially in the DSM-5). They compare behavioral addiction to substance addiction, recount gaming-binge deaths in Taiwan internet cafes, cite the Marshall Carpenter and Quinn Pitcock cases, a 2014 study linking Facebook use to divorce rates, and Susan Mueller's 24-hour unplugged study. They describe persuasive design (B.J. Fogg, Nir Eyal's Hooked, Tristan Harris, Snapchat streaks, notification color, bottomless bowl) and offer tips for cutting back. The episode closes with a listener mail correcting their treatment of the American colonial sugar tax and a plug for the website.

entities.name: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products

segments.title: Opening banter and San Francisco Sketch Fest plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote a San Francisco Sketch Fest show, then introduce the episode on computer addiction and joke about porn theaters and the Georgia Theatre.

segments.title: Defining computer addiction and the DSM debate
segments.summary: The hosts define computer addiction as an umbrella covering porn, gaming, gambling, social media, and smartphone use. They note Internet Addiction Disorder is not in the DSM-5, that the research is mixed, and debate whether behavioral addictions are impulse-control failures or work through dopamine like drugs.

segments.title: Addiction symptoms compared to drug addiction
segments.summary: The hosts go through symptoms of computer addiction that mirror substance addiction, such as losing track of time, failed attempts to cut back, and preoccupation. They discuss Chuck's personal experience quitting video games after a Star Wars game.

segments.title: Gaming binge deaths and Taiwan internet cafes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss deaths linked to gaming binges, especially three deaths in Taiwan internet cafes in 2000. Causes include blood clots from immobility, smoking, caffeine, humidity, and poor health habits. They mention a book called Death by Video Game and note that other gamers kept playing while a body was removed.

segments.title: Online friendships, bar anecdote and social isolation
segments.summary: Josh describes a bar visit where everyone was on their phones and no one talked. They discuss whether online friends can replace in-person ones and whether technology makes people more socially isolated.

segments.title: Gamers who lost careers and the Facebook divorce study
segments.summary: The hosts describe an ESPN Outside the Lines report on Marshall Carpenter, a University of Michigan wrestler who gamed 8 to 14 hours a day, and Quinn Pitcock, who quit the NFL to play Call of Duty. They discuss a 2014 study in Computers in Human Behavior linking annual Facebook growth to divorce rate increases, and compare internet use to TV viewing.

segments.title: Elvis tangent and the 24-hour unplugged study
segments.summary: A tangent about Elvis Presley and his drug use and his meeting with Nixon leads into Susan Mueller's University of Maryland study, in which 200 students gave up media for 24 hours and all said they could not function. The hosts note the study's limits and that technology is necessary for work and news.

segments.title: Persuasive design and habit-forming apps
segments.summary: The hosts explain B.J. Fogg's behavior model (motivation, ability, trigger) from his Stanford lab and Nir Eyal's book Hooked. They describe how triggers like boredom and notifications, red alert colors, LinkedIn's network wheel, Snapchat streaks, and autoplay and infinite feeds are designed to build habits. They cite Tristan Harris's warnings about manipulation.

segments.title: Tips for cutting back and closing research thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts suggest treatment options such as twelve-step programs and interventions for serious cases, plus practical tips like keeping the computer in a high-traffic area. They note that busy people have less time for excessive use. They close by encouraging more in-person conversation.

segments.title: Listener mail on the colonial sugar tax and the outro
segments.summary: A listener from Oklahoma named Thomas corrects the show's syntax episode, explaining that colonial taxes funded the French and Indian War. Josh and Chuck thank him, then promote social media accounts and the website.
